setter.name: Kim Forbes-Sobers
setter.evidence: Named three times by the rep, who used the setter's notes throughout: 'I already got a lot of information from Kim, but I just want to do it the old-fashioned way' (00:04:20); 'Kim also told me that you're a little bit scared of death, you mentioned' (00:16:57); 'I heard from Kim that you had something coming in with like a crypto check' (00:56:13).

prospect.name: Craig
prospect.aka: Joined from a phone; the speaker label throughout is 'iPhone'. Named by the rep repeatedly — 'Great speaking to you, Craig'.
prospect.location: Gillette, Wyoming, USA; previously long-resident in Hawaii
prospect.occupation: Not working. On disability and social security, roughly $2,000 a month. Full-time carer for his 85-year-old father, who has dementia. Formerly in the resort hotel business in Hawaii providing business and convention services, and a scuba diving instructor by trade.
prospect.family_status: Divorced. Two grown daughters and two grandchildren aged seven and four, normally in Hawaii and currently in Wyoming. Lives with and cares for his father. Describes friendships and past relationships internationally, including four years with a partner in Thailand.
prospect.training_background: Lifelong athlete and self-described gym rat until COVID. College wrestler, five-sport letterman, scuba instructor, keen mountain biker in Hawaii, and doing CrossFit in what he calls some of the best shape of his life before a near two-year lockdown. Has also done P90X, extensive yoga and heavy lifting, and has used kettlebells within CrossFit. Currently does no training at all and reports losing muscle mass. Says he has never been able to self-programme — 'I'm not the one to go into the gym and come up with my own routines' — which is why the structure and camaraderie of CrossFit suited him.
prospect.medical: Diagnosed with chronic kidney failure roughly a year ago, described by him as stage five, and currently on in-centre haemodialysis Monday, Wednesday and Friday for four hours, with an indwelling catheter. Suffers what he says a doctor called equilibrium syndrome after each session: profound fatigue, confusion, difficulty remembering names and articulating, lasting until the following day. He has had two car collisions attributed to it and now has a personal rule of driving straight home and lying down for four to six hours. Reports feeling well on two to three days a week only. Earlier history: diagnosed with minimal change disease in Hawaii around three years ago after gaining roughly 20 lb of fluid in days, treated and resolved, then recurred in Wyoming after stopping medication. Two kidney biopsies. His nephrologist says a transplant is required. Prior history of heavy drinking, by his own account up to one or two bottles of wine a day for a period, which he believes contributed and his doctor disputes. Also reports a previously broken fingertip and a tendency to tighten up without stretching. He disputes his diagnosis — 'I'm not sold on the fact that I have what they have diagnosed me with' — and is pursuing two alternatives: a possible transplant in India, which his own doctor endorsed, and an Ayurvedic practitioner he calls Dr Nancy at a clinic he names as Karma Ayurveda, to whom he has already committed $2,000 and who he says can heal his kidneys without dialysis or transplant. Renal dietary restriction is on his mind — he raised potassium limits himself. No clinician was consulted or referenced regarding exercise at any point on this call.

signals: In the middle of a serious active health event rather than recovering from one: on dialysis three days a week with a catheter, stage five chronic kidney failure

Training framed explicitly as part of fighting it — 'I would rather trade four hours of dialysis, three days a week, for four hours of kettlebell' and 'I've been scared into a position where it's almost like a prescription. This is something you have to do, Craig'
Motivation is extremely high and price resistance is absent in principle: 'you don't have to convince me that this is something I need to do or that I want to do. I want to do it'

Refusing to accept the medical prognosis — 'doing dialysis for the rest of my life, or waiting for a transplant, ain't happening, bro. That's not going to happen. I'm going to take action' — which is precisely the profile the spec identifies as easiest to close and most important to screen clinically

goals.text: Rebuild strength and stop losing muscle mass — 'I'm just losing my muscle mass... I'm still strong, I have the desire'
Reduce the post-dialysis disequilibrium and reclaim the four days a week he currently loses to it
Be an active grandfather to grandchildren of seven and four — 'I don't want to be the grandpa that is sitting in a wheelchair, having to be toted around with oxygen'
Not end up like his father, whom he watches daily — 'I look at my dad and I'm looking into a window of the future. And I'm like, I don't want to be like this'
Act before it is too late — 'I don't want to go on too much longer and then look back when I'm 65 or 70 and just be beyond help'
Regain mental stability and stop the cognitive fog — 'I think mentally I need to do something like this. I'm really mentally kind of losing my [grip]'
Look and feel the way he did four or five years ago — 'I don't wish I could get that back. I want to get that back'
Have externally imposed structure and someone to push him — 'I need somebody there to go, all right, Craig, let's get busy'
Regain the flexibility he had from years of yoga; gets very tight without daily movement
Travel and dive again — a trip to see a diving friend in Florida, and a stated desire to dive in the Philippines

pains.text: Stage five chronic kidney failure requiring four-hour haemodialysis three times a week with an indwelling catheter
Post-dialysis disequilibrium syndrome producing confusion, memory and speech difficulty and an indescribable fatigue lasting until the next day; has caused two car collisions
Doing no exercise at all and losing muscle mass
Lifelong pattern of abandoning programmes at the three-to-four-month mark when something in life triggers it — 'then I fall off the rails'
Cannot self-programme and has no external structure since losing CrossFit — 'there were people there to motivate and to have camaraderie, but I don't have that anymore'
Fixed income of about $2,000 a month with roughly $400 liquid and substantial medical bills
Full-time carer for a father with dementia who follows him around the house and constrains his space to train
Fear of death, disclosed to the setter before the call and raised by the rep
Anxiety that training used to manage — 'I really needed to work out just for my own anxiety and my own peace of mind... I lost that center'
Unhappy with where he lives and isolated from the life he wants — 'I hated where I'm at, I don't like being where I'm at right now'
History of heavy drinking, by his own account up to two bottles of wine a day for a period, which he believes contributed to his decline
Car unreliable for about eighteen months, compounding the difficulty of getting to a gym
Sensitive to comments about his condition from people who knew him as an athlete — 'hey, you're putting on a little weight there... I hate that'

objections.raw_quote: I know this, you know, nothing's for free. I'm on a, at the moment, I'm on a fixed income, and I earn about $2,000 a month. I don't have any, well, I have medical bills out the [wazoo]
objections.rep_response: Asked what he had available and was told 'right now I have about 400 bucks to my name'. Acknowledged 'it sounds like for now it might not be the most possible thing because it is in the four figures', then referenced the setter's note about incoming money and continued to the full presentation and the $6,000 price.

objections.raw_quote: I'm committed to two things this month, and so after this month, the following month, which would be September, I haven't been on a proper holiday for about six years, and I'm trying to go down to see a buddy of mine in Florida for a couple of weeks, and so I'm trying to budget for that.
objections.rep_response: Did not run a timing play. Asked when the crypto position would resolve, agreed two calendar checkpoints (end of August and mid-September), and closed the call out.

objections.raw_quote: I'm also in touch with a lady who, her name is Dr. Nancy... And I'm going to start a regimen with her of herbs, diet, and she's even said, you choose the exercise. She wants to incorporate exercise into this. She says, I can heal your kidney problems without dialysis, or without dialysis and without a transplant. So I'm going down that road, too.
objections.rep_response: Probed the prospect's own conviction once — 'It doesn't sound like you 100% believe it, but it could be me' — and when the prospect defended it and disputed his own diagnosis, the rep replied 'I get it. I get it. No, I do. You can never 100% trust it.' No competing clinical position was offered and the $2,000 already committed to that practitioner was never treated as a competing spend.

objections.raw_quote: here's what happens, I'm really hard, it's hard for me over my lifetime, and I don't know why this is, but I'll get into something and I get into it, and then about three or four months into it, there's a life something, whatever it might be, something triggers me. And then I fall off the rails
objections.rep_response: Reframed the six-month programme as a permanent change rather than a cycle — 'this is a transformation, this is not something we do for six months and then you just fall off. This is something you have to continue doing for the rest of your life' — and then asked for a commitment: 'Are you ready to commit to yourself to do that, but also to stick to it instead of falling off?'

offer.payment_plan_terms: 'In-house, to be completely open with you, we can only split up into six payments, and I would also come with extra interest, so that would be like $1,200 a month' — a $7,200 total. The rep then asked about a credit limit and did not pursue it. No two- or three-payment option was mentioned, although the same rep offered exactly that to two other prospects within the preceding 48 hours.

evidence: No payment taken and no link sent. The rep explicitly deferred: 'because I really want to help you, of course, make that change, financially, of course, it's just not possible right now.'

Two follow-up checkpoints agreed and entered in the rep's calendar during the call: 'You should come back to me at the end of this month, maybe once, and then the month after to sort of check it' and 'check with me at the end of this month. And then check with me the middle of September.'
Interim actions agreed: the rep to send a video, the prospect to buy a 12-16 kg kettlebell and start training from that video before any coaching begins.

Counter-evidence on intent: intent was total and stated repeatedly — 'you don't have to convince me that this is something I need to do or that I want to do. I want to do it' and 'there's no doubt that a transformation will begin. Yeah, I'm all down.'

Counter-evidence against ever closing: $400 to his name against a $2,000 monthly disability income, $2,000 already committed to an Ayurvedic practitioner, a Florida trip being budgeted for September, medical bills outstanding, and a funding plan that depends entirely on an unrealised crypto withdrawal he has been trying to complete for some time.
outcome.next_step: Rep to send an instructional video; prospect to buy a kettlebell and begin training from it unsupervised. Rep to check in at the end of August and again in mid-September, contingent on the prospect's crypto position resolving.

notable.note: The highest-risk call in this batch by a wide margin and the one a principal should read first. The prospect is on haemodialysis three times a week for stage five kidney failure with an indwelling catheter, suffers post-dialysis confusion severe enough to have caused two car collisions, and was taken through a loaded ballistic kettlebell programme, encouraged to attempt daily mobility work on dialysis days, and advised at the end of the call to buy a 12-16 kg kettlebell and start training from a video immediately. No question was asked at any point about whether his nephrologist or any clinician had cleared exercise. Separately, the prospect disputed his own diagnosis and said he would not accept dialysis or a transplant, describing an Ayurvedic practitioner who claims she can heal his kidneys without either; the rep's response was 'I get it. I get it. No, I do. You can never 100% trust it.' The rep also projected a future in which the prospect would be 'completely healthy' at 65. On the commercial side, the funding route pursued was an unrealised crypto withdrawal flagged in the setter's notes, from a man with $400 to his name on $2,000 a month of disability income, and the only payment plan offered was the six-instalment $7,200 version, which the same rep had told two other prospects that week was the expensive option to avoid. Credit where due: the rep did not close, did not discount, and deferred on affordability grounds.

quality.notes: Severe and sustained inversion — the two speakers are swapped for most of the first four minutes, including the very first line. At 00:00:03 'I'm calling from Gillette, Wyoming' sits under the rep's label but is the prospect's; at 00:01:53 'No, I'm Dutch myself' is under the prospect's label but is the rep's. From roughly 00:47:34 to 00:48:00 the rep's closing question and the prospect's answer share a single block under the prospect's label. The prospect's label is 'iPhone' throughout because he joined from a phone; his name, Craig, appears only when the rep uses it. Transcription is lossy in places and profanity is redacted inconsistently. Roles read from content throughout. Four minutes of unstructured conversation precede the frame.
